CL003-002----.smr_description: On a narrow (c. 60m) isthmus of land connecting the SW end of Illaunmuckinish island with the mainland, dividing Muckinish Bay to the E from the estuary running into Ballyvaughan Bay to the W and overlooked by a moderately steep-sided rise of bare rock and improved pasture to the S. Indicated and named ‘Shanmuckinish Castle’ on the 1842 and 1915 eds. of the OS 6-inch maps. According to Westropp (1895, 280), the tower house is likely to date to the 15th century and was known locally as Shanmuckinish castle to differentiate it from Muckinishnua, another local castle said to have been built three years later. In 1574, it was owned by the O’Loughlins, but in 1584, Turlough O’Loughlin was taken…

CL003-008002-.smr_description: On the W shore of Pouldoody Bay with two small inlets to E and WNW appearing to form natural, but tidal, landing points and higher pastureland rising gently to the S. Located in and to the NNW seaward-side of a bawn (CL003-008001-). Indicated and named ‘Muckinish Castle (in ruins)’ on the 1842 and 1915 eds. of the OS 6-inch maps and as ‘Caisleán Muicinis Nua (Ó Lochlainn)’ on Robinson’s map (1977). The castle is known locally as ‘Muckinish nua’ a name Westropp (1895, 280) attributed to a legend that it was built three years after Seanmuckinish castle (CL003-002----). Westropp tentatively dated its construction to the 15th century and it was recorded as in ruins by 1837 (Lewis 1995 [1837])…

CL005-128001-.smr_description: On a steep rise with a cliff-edge falling away to the W and NW, within a multiperiod field system (CL005-227004-). Indicated and named ‘Glensleade Castle (in ruins)’ on the 1842 and 1916 eds of the OS 6-inch maps. Apart from a short forfeiture to Edmond Barret in 1595, it belonged to the O’Loughlin clan from the late 16th century until the rebellion of 1641 (Ua Croinín and Breen 1997, 59). After the rebellion it passed to Comyns, Macnamaras and Ralph Wilson. It was likely dismantled by the Cromwellian commissioners c. 1654. A poorly surviving tower house of which only sections of the north wall (L 11m; H 3m; T 2m) survive, in which are the remains of a large, squared embrasure (H 1m; Wth…

CL008-087----.smr_description: On a natural rise in hilly pastureland, situated midway along the SE wall of a bawn (CL008-087002-). Overlooked by higher ground to S and SE, but otherwise commanding a panoramic view. Named ‘Doonnagore Castle (in Ruins)’ on the 1842 and 1920 eds. of the OS 6-inch map. Probably built by the O’Connors in the 14th/15th century, by 1570 the castle was under the ownership of Sir Donnel O’Brien. In 1582 Brian MacCahill O’Connor was recorded as the owner, suggesting that perhaps the O’Connors were still living there under the O’Briens (Ua Cróinín and Breen 1997). Toward the end of that century the castle became a possession and residence of the MacClancy family, brehons of the O’Briens of…

CL010-066002-.smr_description: On a low limestone outcrop in pasture near the SW edge of Carran Turlough, and controlling a narrow E-W routeway between two small, fertile valleys to E and W. Labelled ‘Castle in ruins’ on the both first edition (1842) and later, Cassini edition (1920) of the OS 6-inch map. The castle is depicted as a rectangular structure (L c. 17m N-S; Wth c. 15m E-W) with a projecting NE angle on the first edition map but only an L-shaped portion of the N (L c. 9m) and W (L c. 6m) walls are shown surviving on the Cassini edition. Named ‘Caisleán Boirne (Ó Lochlain)’ on Robinson’s map of the Burren (1977). According to Ua Cróinín and Breen (1997), in 1574, this tower house was in the hands of the…

CL011-007003-.smr_description: Situated on the N perimeter of a bawn (CL011-007002-) at the N end of a NNE-SSW oriented rocky ridge (L c. 40m) overlooking a generally flat low-lying semi-karstic area and Lough Bunny c. 320m to the S. Named ‘Cloondooan Castle (in ruins)’ on the 1842 and 1920 eds. of the OS 6-inch map. Situated on the Corofin-Gort road (Bealach-an-Fiadhfhail / Bealach Fiodhfail in medieval records) (Ua Cróinín and Breen 1997; Healy 1998, 65). A stronghold of the O’Brien family, in 1569 Cloondooan (Cluain Dubhain) castle was laid siege to and captured by British Lord Justice Sir Henry Sidney (Ua Cróinín and Breen 1997). In 1580 Mahon O’Brien of Cloondooan led an insurrection against the British, for which…

CL017-084002-.smr_description: Surrounded by a very small 17th-century bawn (CL017-084001-) on a slight rise in level rough pasture, with a possibly associated enclosure (CL017-084003-) immediately to the SW of the bawn, and the remains of a possible cashel (CL017-084004-) just beyond this to the SW. Drawn and named ‘Ballyportry Castle (in ruins)’ and ‘Tower’ on the first edition (1842) of the OS 6-inch map but with the label ‘Tower’ omitted from the later OS 25-inch plan (1897) and Cassini edition (1920) of the OS 6-inch map. According to Ua Cróinín and Breen (1994, 24), this tower house was probably built in the late 15th or early 16th century by the O’Briens of Leamaneh, with the earliest historical mention possibly…

CL034-014002-.smr_description: On a rise in a low-lying landscape. A rectangular 16th-century tower house (ext. dims. 11.6m NE-SW; 9.4m NW-SE) surviving to two storeys beneath a barrel vault (H 12m). A 1604 Inquisition at Clarecastle, finds that Conor, son of Daniel O'Brien, late of “Castletown Macrossy” owned at the time of his death the upper room of the castle, the cellar, parts of the bawn, the orchard of the…

CL035-028----.smr_description: In pasture, on a low rise, in an undulating landscape with good views to W and reasonable views to N and S. Named ‘Garruragh Castle’ on the 1921 OS 6-inch map. A 2/3 storey rectangular tower house (max. ext. dims. 11.2m N-S; 7.5m E-W) of roughly squared and coursed limestone, having a base-batter (Wth 0.25m; H 2.75m). Ua Cróinín and Breen (1997) indicate that the castle was built c. 1440-1480 by Donnchad MacNamara and it remained in the family until 1641 when it was granted to Philip Bigoe. According to Salter (2004, 37) the structure was in use as a fever hospital in the 1840s. This is probably due to its proximity to Tulla Union Workhouse, which is c. 640m to SW. CL035-055002-.smr_description: On top of a rectangular limestone rock outcrop (CL035-055001-), in rough pasture with reasonable views in all directions, across a gently undulating landscape. Named ‘Lissofin Castle’ on the 1841 and 1921 edition OS 6-inch maps. According to Curry in 1839, Lissofin is Anglicised from Lis-Aodha-Finn referring to the Fort of Hugh the Fair (OSL, vol. 2, 284). Lissofin castle was a McNamara stronghold associated with McNamara Finn who was an ancestor of Hugh the Fair. CO001-021----.smr_description: At the W end of a low plateau; the ground falls away to the N, W and S. The original form of this keepless 13th-century castle was probably a square ward enclosed by a curtain wall with a circular tower at each corner, but only the SW curtain wall (L 38m), the S and W towers, and a length of the NW wall (L 29.8m) now stand (see plan in McNeill 1997, 140). It is an example of an 'enclosure' castle. The curtain wall (H c. 6m; T 1.8m) and towers were built of random rubble, with a pronounced low base batter. Parts of the deep moat that would have surrounded the castle also survive. The remainder of the castle was demolished c. 1696 to provide stone for nearby Kilbolane House (CO001-029----)…

CO033-009001-.smr_description: On a slight limestone eminence, overlooking bridge on the Blackwater River c. 150m to the S. These remains of a fortified house are comprised of a rectangular 3-storey house (int. 25m N-S; 8.3m E-W) with 4-storey towers projecting from the NW and SW corners and from the centre of the E and W walls; the former is polygonal in plan, while the latter have straight sides and pointed front (see plan in Leask 1944, plate 1). The plan by Leask also shows wall foundations within the fortified house but not associated with it, which may be part of the earlier castle of the Fitzgerald earls of Desmond (CO033-009004-) (ibid., 23). The house was built by Sir Thomas Norris, a senior English…

CO039-078001-.smr_description: Now standing at the SE end of an 18th-century country house, built directly on a rock outcrop. This rectangular 5-storey tower with an adjacent circular 2-storey tower was built by the Mac Carthys in 1450, according to tradition (Lee 1914,64), a date not inconsistent with the present remains. The circular turret was added later, probably in the late 16th/early 17th century to allow for flanking fire by defenders. The adjacent house was built by the Wallis family in the 18th century but enlarged and castellated in the mid-19th century (Bence-Jones, 1988, 108). The house later became a convent school, and is now in use as accommodation for asylum seekers. The tower house and turret were…

CO071-096002-.smr_description: In level pasture; rectangular tower (14.65m E-W; 9.7m N-S) with triangular projections or spurs at SW and NE corners (see plan, Gillman 1892b, 234). Now stands to 4 storeys but was at least one floor higher; about 1864 SE corner blown up by 'vandals' (ibid.) so that most of E wall and E half of S wall no longer stand. At ground-floor level, N end of guard chamber survives in thickness of E wall, close to NE corner; indicating probability that tower was entered by door in centre of E wall, with spiral staircase rising in SE corner (no trace of either feature survives). There appears to have been mural chambers in E wall at 1st-, 2nd- and 3rd-floor levels, of which only N end-walls survive…

Walls stand to full height but floors and roofs collapsed and in dangerous condition. Gables atop each elevation of main block and towers; string courses on all elevations between floor levels. Each tower has square chimney stack atop both inward-facing gables, also stack atop main W wall. Bartizan atop outside corner on each tower; each supported by five elegantly tapering corbels (central one set on corner)…

CO093-064----.smr_description: On N bank of Bandon river, ivy-clad four storey rectangular tower (16.2m E-W; 9.7m N-S) built on low rock ridge in flat, marshy area. Entered at ground level by doorway near S end of E wall; lobby inside gives access to main chamber to E (8.45m E-W; 6m N-S); spiral staircase in NE corner rises full height of tower. Tiny unlit chamber (2m x 1.4m) at foot of stairs known locally as 'chambrin á chodaigh (the tyrant's little room)' (Lyons et al. 1895, 483). Unusually, spiral stairs built around central circular masonry column (diam. 0.88m). Ground-floor window opes in N, S and W walls all enlarged by recent use. CO108-051003-.smr_description: On rocky eminence with good view in all directions, overlooking Ballynacarriga Lough to the SW. This four storey tower house (14.6m E-W; 11.8m N-S) is entered through a rebuilt ground-floor door in the E wall; there is a portcullis slot over the door. A vaulted lobby gives access to a guardroom to the S; the main chamber is to the W; a short flight of steps to the N leads to spiral stair in the NE corner which rises the full height of the tower. The area over the lobby is occupied by six chambers, one above the other; the 1st and 2nd floor are entered from the main chambers; otherwise they are entered from the spiral stairs. Windows have square-set embrasures covered by segmental vaults…

CV020-060----.smr_description: Clogh Oughter castle is a large circular tower situated on a tiny island in Lough Oughter, Co. Cavan. It appears to have been built by the Anglo-Norman de Lacys, lords of Meath, about 1220 as part of their attempt to conquer the territory of Bréifne, roughly equivalent to the modern counties of Leitrim and Cavan. The O’Reillys were the lords of East Breifne (Co. Cavan) and the island on which Clogh Oughter was built had been their royal crannog. In early references to the castle it was called the Castle of Crannog O’Reilly. The de Lacys were driven out of this part of East Bréifne by the O’Reillys in 1233 and Clogh Oughter remained mostly in O’Reilly hands from then until about 1608. During…

CV025-113----.smr_description: A three-storey tower house constructed of roughly coursed limestone blocks, with pronounced base batter rising to a height of c. 3m. Remains comprise the E and S walls and featureless N wall. W wall is largely destroyed. Entrance with remains of masonry arch at centre of E wall above which is a well-preserved cut-stone loop. A large opening at ground-floor level flanks doorway on its N side. Fenestration in S wall includes two loops, one placed directly above the other lighting the staircase, a narrow ope with large embrasure at ground-floor level and the remains of a large window-opening at first-floor level. CV036-001----.smr_description: Described as 'Cloone House' on the 1835 and 1876 eds of the OS 6-inch map. This is the SW wall of a late 18th/early 19th-century house with large quantities of brick and no features other than a fireplace and tall window at the ground floor and a fragment of a window at the first. It is believed to have been built on the site of a castle (local information), about which there is no other knowledge. There are no visible remains of any earlier structure. The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Cavan' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1995). CV038-019----.smr_description: Situated on a small rocky island, c. 300m from the W shore of Lough Sheelin. Constructed in the late 14th century by Thomas McMahon O'Reilly. Davies described it as a two-storey rectangular tower with base batter, a barrel vault over the ground floor and remains of a doorway in S wall. Intramural staircases occur in E wall leading to first floor, and in N wall leading to roof level. Site is densely overgrown with vegetation. The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Cavan' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1995). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research. Date of upload/revision: 22 December 2008

CV039-055----.smr_description: Situated on a small promontory jutting into Lough Ramor and cut off from the mainland by a substantial external bank and wide, deep fosse curving from NE-E-SE. The motte is situated in the SE of the enclosed area. It comprises a high, steep-sided, and flat-topped circular earthen mound (diam. of base c. 28m; H 4-5m). The summit of the mound is also circular (diam. c. 12m N-S). A shallow fosse to the NE of the motte separates it from the bailey which itself comprises two courts separated by a low stone wall. The outer court adjoins a rectangular depression which may have been a slipway for boats. No trace of any buildings within bailey. (Davies 1947a, 78) The above description is derived…

DG046-004----.smr_description: Inch Castle: First mentioned in 1454, this tower house was probably in ruins by 1600. It was granted to Chichester at the time of the Plantation and although his tenant Mr. Skinner had 'pr' pared lyme and other materials to rebuyld the Castle' the remains do not indicate that he made any alterations (Davies and Swan 1939, 205-6; Hunter 1975, 82). Situated on a small ridge on the SW shore of the island, Inch Castle is protected by a cliff on the S and W and a steep slope on the N; the ridge has been quarried to a cliff face on the E, probably both as a defence and for building stone. GA007-062001-.smr_description: On a rise overlooking a bridging point on E bank of a small stream, probably on or close to the site of an earlier castle (GA007-062----). This well-preserved semi-fortified 17th-C house, now a Nat. Mon., was probably built by the Burke family c. 1630 (Harbison 1975, 92-3; Bence-Jones 1978, 141). Rectangular in ground plan (ENE-WSW; L 19m, Wth 10.5m), it consists of three storeys over a basement (Craig 1982, 132-3). The main doorway, at first-floor level in S wall, is set into W side of a deeply recessed centre bay. GA016-021----.smr_description: In flat pastureland, now partially planted with conifers. This Nat. Mon. is known locally as 'Jenning's Castle'. According to Harbison (1975, 91), it was built by the de Burgos in the late 16th or 17th C. It comprises a very well-preserved rectangular five-storey tower (L 12.2m, Wth 9.8m) which is built on a plinth. A series of (?)modern steps lead to the finely dressed pointed arch doorway near N end of E wall: probably a later insertion of 17th-C date. The doorway is flanked by two small loops, possibly for guns, though the presence of an iron hinge in one jamb suggests that it was once guarded by an iron grill. The doorway opens into a lobby from which access is gained to a guardroom to…

GA036-001001-.smr_description: On an island in Ballynahinch Lake, reputedly the site of an earlier habitation (GA036-001002-). In existence in 1574 when it was in the possession of 'Donell Ecowga' O'Flaherty (Nolan 1901, 116), and reputedly built by him with stones from Toombeola Abbey (GA050-026001-). It consists of a small, rectangular four-storey tower (L 9.1m, Wth 6.5-7m). The interior was extensively altered in the 18th C when a two-storey extension containing kilns was added on W side. The original entrance is in E wall with spiral stairs in SE corner. There is an intramural latrine passage in S wall of 1st floor. The 2nd floor has been extensively remodelled. Mon. consists of a 16th-17th-C tower house enclosed by two bawns: a large, irregular outer bawn (46m by 49m), lying to S and E of the tower house, is defended by five turrets. The remains of a rectangular banqueting hall (L 24m, Wth >7m) stand in its SW corner. The earlier, wedge-shaped inner bawn (36m by 22m max.) sits on the rock outcrop and was defended by a drawbridge, gun loops and a circular turret at SE corner, the latter later reused as a dovecote. Immediately adjoining this, at the same level, are the springings of a narrow stone vault running NW-SE: possibly to support a latrine passage between 2nd/3rd floors. A doorway in S corner on 1st floor probably gives access to the angled bartizan which is visible externally on this corner. All the windows are rectangular with flat heads. An intramural stairs to S leads to the 1st floor from where the spiral stairs rises in SE angle to 3rd floor. Another spiral stairs in SW angle of this floor leads to roof level. GA069-002----.smr_description: On S shore of a small bay on E side of Lough Corrib. Nolan (1901a, 42), quoting from Parker, notes that 'the existence of a castle [GA069-002----] at this spot seems to have sprung from the desire of the Archbishops of Tuam to suppress the bishopric of Annaghdown'. The last bishop was appointed here in 1421 and 'it is to him that the erection of the present castle in probably due' (ibid). In 1574 'Anaghocyne' was in the possession of 'Nicholas Lynch' (Nolan 1901b, 118). An almost square tower (L 11m, Wth 10.3m), in fair condition, it is five storeys high. LA034-019002-.smr_description: Part of N wall and NE angle survive of this two-storey high tower house (dims. 7.3m N-S, 8m E-W) which is built of roughly coursed limestone rubble. Evidence of the bawn (LA034-019013) (dims. 22m N-S, 27m E-W) to N and S defined by a low bank (Wth. c. 4m) and outer fosse. Numerous earthworks in the field to N, S and W of the castle may be of medieval date. LA035-022001-.smr_description: Erected by the MacGillapatricks c. 1425; damaged by the Crowellians in the mid seventeenth century and left uninhabitable (Carrigan 1905 vol. 2, 231-3). Mural stairwell in NE angle. There is a N-S barrel vault over the ground floor with evidence of a loft which was accessed from an opening in N wall. Mural passage on first and second floors of S wall, and chambers in SE and SW angles, with remains of wicker-centring in SE ones. Large cut-limestone fireplace on second floor of E wall. LE002-014002-.smr_description: Built on the S side of crannóg (LE002-01401-), which is located c. 100m off the S shore of Lough Melvin close to Rosclogher church (LE002-015001-), which is c. 120m to the S. LE035-012----.smr_description: Situated in woodland c. 25m from the E shore of Lough Rinn, which is described as ‘Clam Lough’ on the Down Survey (1656-8) barony map where the castle is depicted as what might be two towers. LF016-018001-.smr_description: Within the interior of a possible early medieval ringwork (LF016-018003-) that was subsequently reused as a bawn (LF016-018002-). Possibly the residence of Thomas Nugent, one of the commissioners for Plantation of Longford in 1620 (Cal. pat. rolls Ire., Jas I, 469). This fortified house (overall ext. dims. 23.3m N–S; 10.75m E–W) consisted of a two-storey block with an adjoining four-storey tower at its N end. Only fragmentary remains of the walls (max. LF023-113001-.smr_description: On the SE corner of the claustral range of buildings of the Cistercian abbey (LF023-113----) and within a graveyard (LF023-113016-). This four-storey tower house (ext. dims. 5.8m E–W; 5.4m N–S) is built of roughly coursed rubble and is densely overgrown with ivy. The S and W walls have collapsed and survive only to the first-floor level. The doorway was probably in the N wall close to the NE angle but this area is obscured by collapse. The partially collapsed spiral stairwell is in this angle and it accessed each floor level via a mural passage. There is a barrel vault over the inaccessible ground floor. LH005-042005-.smr_description: Usually referred to as 'Taaffe's Castle', it is four storeys high, excluding the wall-walk level, and is constructed of roughly coursed greywacke and limestone rubble and boulders with a very few hammer- or punch-dressed blocks, but with some finely dressed quoin stones. It is rectangular in plan with a westward projecting tower at the SW angle which carries the stairwell. The main doorway, situated in the W end of the S wall, has a two-centred arch constructed of nine large blocks of dressed limestone. The upper parts of the castle are not now generally accessible because it is used as a private warehouse, but it was surveyed by Ms B. Cassidy for a B.A. thesis at Queen's University…

LH012-061001-.smr_description: Built of limestone and greywacke boulders, slabs and blocks, with projecting towers at the W and E angles. The castle is so orientated that each angle more or less coincides with a point of the compass, but for convenience the NE façade is taken as the N wall, SW as S, etc. The towers on the diagonally opposing angles project in one direction only: that at the NE contains the remains of the stairwell while the one at the SW has the garderobes. Entry to the tower house is gained at present through a modern doorway in the E angle-tower but the original entrance is just to the S of it in the E wall. This doorway originally led to the barrel-vaulted area and to the stairwell immediately N of…

LH017-101015-.smr_description: Known as 'Hatch's Castle', four storeys high and sub-rectangular in plan, it is constructed of uncoursed limestone rubble and greywacke. It is lived in and has been thoroughly modernised leaving little evidence of the original doors or windows. Access to the castle is now through the modern doorway in the centre of the W wall but the original entrance was at the E end of the S wall. This gave access to the stairwell, which was in the SW angle-tower, and to the barrel-vaulted area of the ground floor. The doorway to the stairwell has a two-centred arch and is constructed of hammer-dressed…

LH017-101018-.smr_description: ('The Courthouse') Almost rectangular in plan with westward-projecting towers at the NW and SW angles, it is constructed of roughly coursed limestone blocks, boulders and greywacke. LH018-040----.smr_description: Built of roughly coursed limestone and greywacke rubble with limestone quoins, vertically set. It has a slight batter and is three storeys high over a N-S barrel vault. LI005-017004-.smr_description: National monument No. 383. Ground floor has broad embrasures with narrow round openings on each of the surviving walls. E corner has remnants of spiral stairs; alcove on NE wall. The only features are double-splay lights in the E and W walls and a passage in the E wall leading to the newel stairs in the NE tower. According to the Civil Survey (1654-6) Edward Scurlock of Frane in Athboy parish owned 312 acres there in 1640 and the property included ‘two waste castles and a hall and a quarry, and some cottages’ (Simington 1940, 209). ME032-047002-.smr_description: Situated on a S-facing slope of Skreen Hill. The motte at Skreen (ME032-047001-), located c. 80m to the SSW, became the caput of the de Feipo manor of Skreen (Otway-Ruthven 1964, 117), but at some stage a tower house was built. According to the Civil Survey (1654-6) Thomas Nugent of Rosse and others including Francis Dillon of Proudstown owned 640 acres at Skreen, of which Thomas owned the greater part. Ballintober Castle was built by Richard de Burgh, the second Earl of Ulster known as the Red Earl, c. 1300 (Claffey 1972-3; 1974-5), and it is first mentioned in 1315 when it was captured by Ruaraí O'Conor. It was described in an inquisition of 1333 as surrounded by a stone wall with ruinous buildings, a hall, a chamber, and a kitchen. About 300 acres were worked directly in demesne and there were free tenants in the territory of Síl Mael Ruain, which extended off to the NW (Knox 1903, 59-60). In 1362 Cathal Óg O’Conor seized the castle, and it was retained by one branch or another of the O'Conors throughout the rest of the Middle Ages…

RO041-048001-.smr_description: On the E bank of a NE-SW section of the River Suck, at a point where it turns W. What is described as a bawn (RO041-084002-) at Athliag Maenagan in Hy Many was destroyed by Ulick Mac William Burke in 1487 (AFM vol. 4, 1153). Only the ivy-covered E corner of a four storey structure survives with a grass-covered cairn (dims 27m ENE-WSW; 22m NNW-SSE; H up to 3m) at its base.
